evidence: Cic. Att. 13.7.1: Lentulum cum Metellā certē fēcisse dīvortium (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: The divorce itself; “to divorce someone” is dīvortium facere cum aliquō (aliquā), as Cicero writes of Lentulus and Metella (Traupman 194 and Morgan–Owens give the same phrase). From dīvertere, to go different ways: the word also means a fork in a road, and dīvortium aquārum a watershed (Cic. Att. 5.20.3).

terms.gloss: to divorce (one’s wife), to send her notice of divorce
evidence: Cic. de Or. 1.183; Att. 1.13.3 (Lewis & Short, s.v. nūntius)
terms.comment: The act of divorcing, said by Cicero of a husband and also of a wife who leaves her husband (Top. 19). Nūntius here is the message, not the messenger.

terms.gloss: repudiation; the breaking off of a marriage or an engagement
terms.register: the legal word; in comedy of breaking off a betrothal (Plaut., Ter.)
evidence: Plaut. Aul. 4.10.69; Ter. Phorm. 5.7.35: repudium remittere (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: The jurists distinguish it from dīvortium: an engagement can be broken off by repudium but not by dīvortium. Cicero uses only dīvortium (Lewis & Short).

phrases.latin: Lentulum cum Metellā certē fēcisse dīvortium
phrases.english: that Lentulus has certainly divorced Metella
on divorce the dowry would have to be returned to the wife
